components.html:
There are many variables when knitting (both by hand and by machine).  
  • Different colors of the SAME yarn may knit to a different gauge
  • Different dye lots of the SAME color of the SAME yarn may knit to a different gauge
  • Different models of the SAME gauge knitting machine may knit to a different gauge.
  • The SAME size knitting needle from a different manufacturer may knit to a different gauge
  • Different people, using the exactly the SAME needles, machines, and yarns may get get different gauges
SWATCHING IS NOT OPTIONAL!
How many times have you knit something that just didn't fit?  Have you ever had colors run or fade when you washed your sweater?
So many knitting disasters can be avoided by swatching and dressing your swatch.  Machine knitters have NO EXCUSE for not swatching!  We can knit multiple swatches quickly, testing stitch patterns and tensions.  Since we don't have a lot of time invested, we can do the "throw-the-swatch-in-the-wash-with-jeans" test to see if a washable yarn will hold up.

DRESSING A SWATCH
To dress a swatch, wash/steam/block the swatch as you will care for the finished garment.
Dressing gives you a feel for how the fiber in the yarn will appear in the finished garment. It allows you to check for colorfastness and hand.
The ONLY way to get an accurate knitting gauge is to dress your swatches. Only then will you get an accurate gauge.

Don't panic!
Every machine knitter has experienced this:
 
  • You dutifully knit, dress and measure your swatch.
  • You cast on and knit the back of your sweater
  • You bind off that last stitch and are really excited
  • The piece looks a bit funny and you start to measure.
UH OH! The dimensions aren't right .....
Don't panic!
When we knit on the machine, the stitches are stretched between the needles. We also add weight. All of this distorts the knitting.
Remember
  • You let the swatch rest before you measured.... let the piece rest as well.
  • You dressed your swatch and there may have been some shrinkage ... you won't have accurate measurements of your piece until it's washed.

Try it yourself

The next time you knit a swatch:
  1. Measure it immediately after it comes off the machine and record the length and width.
  2. Wait a few hours and measure and record again
  3. Wait overnight and measure one more time.
You will be surprised at the difference!

Measuring your swatch to find the correct gauge is the most important step in making sure your garment will fit. Gauge rulers make it easier to measure gauge from your swatch.
Follow your manual and knit a swatch with stitches and rows marked as instructed.
Stitches:
  • Place the ruler with the "S" side up aligned with the STITCHES of your swatch
  • Place the edge of the ruler against the stitch yarn mark
  • Read across the ruler to the opposite yarn mark
  • This indicates the stitches in 4" (10cm)
Rows:
  • Place the ruler with the "R" side up aligned with the ROWS of your swatch
  • Place the edge of the ruler against the row yarn mark where the contrasting color meets the main color
  • Read across the ruler to the opposite row marker (where the contrasting color meets the main color)
  • The number indicates the Rows in 4" (10cm)
For 4.5 standard gauge use the GREEN gauge ruler. Isolate 40 stitches and 60 rows
For Mid-gauge Machines use the YELLOW gauge ruler. Isolate 30 stitches and 40 rows
For 9.0 Bulky Gauge use the BLUE gauge ruler. Isolate 20 stitches and 30 rows
Of course, a regular ruler works too!

GAUGE SWATCH for matching gauge

I recently had an epiphany about swatching when I'm trying to MATCH gauge.  In the past I've knit my gauge swatches as I learned as a machine knitter.   I never use the gauge rulers that came with my machines, but I've always knit my swatches according to the "rules". (DUH)
On my standard machine, I've dutifully cast on 60 stitches and knit 60 rows between marked rows .  I marked off 40 stitches and got out my regular ruler, measured and did the math.
Being a total non-math person, I can't tell you how many times I've messed up the calculation of my gauge ... even when using a calculator.
THE EPIPHANY: I was hand knitting a HK pattern.  Hand knitting the complicated sections of the pattern was fun, but I decided that knitting a whole lot of stockinette (the boring stuff by hand) was dumb.  So I threaded up my machine and started to knit a swatch. The gauge I needed to match was 24 sts and 30 rows per 4".
  •  I cast 60 stitches (so I could easily measure 24 stitches)
  •  I knit a few rows with my main yarn (recording the tension with eyelets)
  •  2 rows of a contrasting color
  •  Knit 30 rows
  •  2 rows of a contrasting color
  •  A few main yarn rows and bound off
  • AT THE SAME TIME I also marked  the stitches that were framing my desired 24 stitches.
In other words, instead of marking the traditional number of stitches and rows, I broke the "rules" and marked my DESIRED GAUGE  of 24 stitches and 30 rows as I knit the swatch.
I let the swatch rest, then wet blocked it and let it sit overnight. The next day, I put my handy-dandy 4" measuring tool down on my swatch.  (see below about my DIY 4" tool)

Stitch Gauge is close - but the row gauge is off

Success!
As you can see, by the first photo, my stitch gauge was good, but my row gauge needed to be adjusted.  It was easy to see through my tool that I had too many rows to 4".   I adjusted my mast tension, knit another swatch and VOILA!  I was able to match my gauge EXACTLY --- with NO MATH!
DIY 4" Swatch tool
For my tool, I cut a 4" x 4" square of quilters template plastic (readily available at craft stores) to create my Handy-dandy tool. Because it's see-through, I can see my marked stitches and rows on my swatch.
You could use a square of any material (cardboard, paper, clear plastic of any kind).
We've created a to-scale template for you to print. Print the template on paper, a transparency or card stock and try it.  I think you will be amazed at how much easier it is to measure gauge (for both hand and machine knitting).

components.html:
Instructions are for suggestions for standard gauge (mid-gauge, bulky) and for using gauge rulers.
Remember, you can knit swatches any size (as long as they are at least 5-6" square.) Be sure to be consistent and establish a template for yourself for every time you knit a swatch.
  1. Cast on 60(50,30) stitches (add extra stitches so you can measure the center without edge distortion.)
  2. Knit a few rows in pattern
  3. Knit 2 rows in waste yarn (or weave a marker row)
  4. Set row counter to 000
  5. Knit the center section
    Standard gauge: total of 60 rows)
    • Knit 20 rows and knit in a yarn marker isolating the center 40 stitches
    • Knit 20 more rows and place a marker on the same needles
    • Knit 20 more rows
    Mid-Gauge: (total of 40 rows)
    • Knit 20 rows and knit in a yarn marker isolating the center 30 stitches
    • Knit 20 more rows and place a marker on the same needles
    Bulky (total of 30 rows)
    • Knit 15 rows and knit in a yarn marker isolating the center 40 stitches
    • Knit 15 more rows
  6. Confirm and record the total number of rows you knit for the center 60(40, 30)
  7. Knit 2 rows in waste yarn (or weave a marker row)
  8. Knit a few rows and bind off (or drop the work from the machine)
Let the swatch rest
  1. Dress the swatch as you will treat the finished item
  2. Measure the size of the 40(30, 20) stitches in the center of the swatch (between the yarn markers)
  3. Measure the size of the 60(40,30) rows between the waste yarn (or marker rows)
  4. The math
    • Divide the stitches in the middle by your measurement to get Stitches Per Inch/cm
    • Divide the rows in the middle by your measurement to get Rows Per Inch/cm
    • Multiply your stitches/rows per inch/cm times 4 to calculate stitches per 4" (10cm)

Knitting Machine Gauge and Tension

Carriage and Mast Tension Dials

  • Maybe you want to keep out the cold with a thick, tight knitted fabric for warm hats and mittens.
  • A loose, open, drapey fabric may be just the ticket for a sweater or shawl
With a little experimenting you can have these and everything in between
Think of the Carriage Tension Dial as the hand knitting needle size.
Think of the Mast Tension Dial as the tension a hand knitter would apply to the yarn with her fingers

The Stitch Dial on your carriage controls how the yarn passes through the carriage and is placed in the hooks of the needles. A smaller number makes a tight stitch, a larger number makes a loose stitch.

The Mast Tension Dial, along with the yarn guides/tension springs (antennae) control the tension of the yarn as it's fed into the carriage.
Take time to play with tension on your machine. You'll be surprised with the results. Try in Stockinette, but also try different extreme tensions with stitch patterns as well. Get creative!

Instruction are for standard gauge (mid/bulky gauge)
  1. Cast on 60 (30) Stitches
  2. Knit 10 rows at a middle tension appropriate for your machine (i.e. tension 5)
  3. Mark the row (eyelets or a yarn marker)
  4. Change the tension -2 full numbers (i.e. tension 3)
  5. Knit 30 rows
  6. Mark the row (eyelets or a yarn marker)
  7. Change the tension +4 full numbers (i.e. tension 7)
  8. Knit 30 rows
  9. Continue playing with the tension if desired
  10. Drop the work from the machine or bind off
    11. Examine the differences in the tensions and determine which you prefer.
    Can you see design possibilities here?

If you haven't used your chosen yarn before, how do you know the best tension to knit your sweater?
  Knitters tend to use the terms "tension swatch" and "gauge swatch" interchangeably, lets take a look at both.

GAUGE SWATCH

The gauge swatch is the "official" swatch used when designing a garment.
It is knit at a specific size, marked for accurate stitch and row measurement and "dressed" as the final garment will be treated.
TIP: Whatever method you use to create a swatch, the key is to correctly measure it and calculate your gauge.

TENSION SWATCH

When I pick up a new cone of yarn, I can't wait to thread up my machine and see what the yarn looks like.   From the initial cast on, I start guessing what setting on my tension dial I need to use.  I knit a few inches and reach down and start to feel the resulting fabric.
Once I get a feel for the yarn (what machine, general tension setting at stockinette, etc) I create a tension swatch.  This helps me fine-tune the tension needed to achieve the fabric I like and allows me to play with various techniques.  I'm often very surprised that a yarn looks great in tuck, and awful in slip, for example.  Adding a few eyelets here and there tells me if the yarn will work up in lace.
Let's practice knitting a tension swatch.

Try it yourself
  1. Play!
  2. Start knitting stockenette at the tightest tension that will knit.  (If the tension is too tight, you'll see stitches that don't form properly.
  3. Knit 2-4 inches. Knit a marker row (change colors, work a few eyelets across the row or knit a sewing thread in with the main yarn)
  4. Keep knitting sections, marking the tension dial number in each section.  Knit the last section as loosely as possiblle, even if you think this will be too loose ... I'm often very pleasantly surprised at the result.
  5. Transfer every other needle to out of work postion and knit a section - put all needles back into work.
  6. Work a simple tuck, or slip, or any stitch pattern of your choice ... base your tension dial setting on the stockinette sections you just knit.
The point of this exercise is to put the yarn through it's paces ... ignite your creativity, and get a feel for what the yarn can do.  If you don't have a huge cone, you can always re-wind this knitting. At this point, you probably know exactly what you want to do with this yarn.  Knit your Gauge Swatch, dress it and and you are ready to design and knit your sweater.

It is important that you know how to estimate yarn for all of your knitting projects
(hint: it's based on your swatch and a little math)
